author: Amphilochius of Iconium
occasion: A sermon on the Gospel story of Zacchaeus, encouraging sinners to run to repentance by showing Christ's mercy to tax collectors and sinners.
argument: Amphilochius argues that nothing raises the soul to joy like fear of God, turning from evil, and repentance, and that all the saved—prophets, apostles, evangelists—drew from the same mercy of Christ. He presents Zacchaeus the chief tax collector as a model of repentance: a man trapped by greed and injustice who sought to see Jesus, climbed a tree, and was called and transformed by Christ. The sermon compares the barren, deadly spring of Jericho healed by Elisha's salt with the church healed by Christ through the apostles, and draws a parallel between Zacchaeus and Rahab, both saved by receiving Jesus. It closes by defending Christ's lodging with sinners and praising Zacchaeus's restitution and poverty as true wealth.

outline.move: The homily opens by praising repentance and shows that David, Peter, Paul, Matthew, and Zacchaeus all drew from Christ's mercy, then introduces Zacchaeus as the day's subject and begins comparing him with Rahab of Jericho.

The barren, deadly spring of Jericho is described and interpreted as the pre-Christian church, healed by Elisha's salt, which prefigures Christ seasoning the church through the apostles; Zacchaeus is then introduced as a chief tax collector who exploited travelers, merchants, and shepherds.

Zacchaeus, small in stature and burdened by injustice, climbs a sycamore to see Jesus, reasoning that if Jesus knows his hidden thoughts he can be saved; Jesus arrives and calls him down, interpreting the descent from the tree as preparation for ascent through the cross.

Jesus declares he must stay at Zacchaeus's house, turning the tax collector's home into paradise; the murmuring critics are rebuked, Zacchaeus promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution, and the homily closes by handing the praise of Zacchaeus's virtues to the father rich in virtues.

cast.name: Zacchaeus
cast.who: A chief tax collector in Jericho who climbs a sycamore to see Jesus and is transformed by receiving him.

cast.name: Jesus
cast.who: The true Jesus, who sees hearts, calls Zacchaeus down, and lodges in his house.

cast.name: Rahab
cast.who: The prostitute of Jericho who received Joshua son of Nun as a spy; a type of Zacchaeus's salvation.

cast.name: Joshua son of Nun
cast.who: The Old Testament Joshua, who led Israel into the promised land; a type of Christ.

cast.name: Elisha
cast.who: The prophet who healed the waters of Jericho with salt, prefiguring Christ healing the church through the apostles.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The prophet who, despite adultery, received forgiveness and pronounced the blessedness of forgiven sinners.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle who denied Christ yet holds the keys of the kingdom.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle who persecuted the church yet became apostle to the Gentiles.

cast.name: Matthew
cast.who: The tax collector called by Jesus; Zacchaeus wishes to imitate him, though Matthew was called and obeyed while Zacchaeus takes initiative.

scripture: The author uses Septuagint book names and numbering. Psalms are cited according to the Septuagint numbering. _unresolved_facts.claim: He presents Zacchaeus the chief tax collector as a model of repentance: a man trapped by greed and injustice who sought to see Jesus, climbed a tree, and was called and transformed by Christ.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀλλ' οὗτος ὁ ἄγροικος, ὁ πένης, ὁ ὄρεσιν προσομιλῶν Ζακχαίῳ περιέπιπτεν δεκατευόμενος τὰ θρέμματα, ἐννόμως λῃστευόμενος, ἄνευ ξίφους ἀναιρούμενος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The sermon emphasizes Zacchaeus as exploiter and oppressor of others (shepherds, merchants, travelers) more than 'trapped by greed and injustice' suggests; he actively preys on others like a drone-bee, and his transformation is framed as Christ's initiative in seeing and calling him, not primarily Zacchaeus's seeking.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The sermon compares the barren, deadly spring of Jericho healed by Elisha's salt with the church healed by Christ through the apostles
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐλθὼν ὁ κύριος τοὺς ἀποστόλους ὡς ἅλας ἐμβαλὼν ἤρτυσεν αὐτὴν καὶ πότιμον ἐποίησεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says the Lord came and 'threw in the apostles as salt' (ἐμβαλὼν), not 'Christ through the apostles'; the apostles are the salt itself, not instruments through which Christ works separately.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The homily opens by praising repentance and shows that David, Peter, Paul, Matthew, and Zacchaeus all drew from Christ's mercy, then introduces Zacchaeus as the day's subject and begins comparing him with Rahab of Jericho.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐν γὰρ τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις οὐ Ματθαῖον μόνον σῳζόμενον ἐκ τελωνῶν οἶδα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑτέρους σὺν αὐτῷ δύο· ὧν εἷς μὲν προσευχόμενος ἐκ τοῦ τὸ στῆθος τύπτειν... Ζακχαῖος δὲ ἀνελθὼν ἐπὶ τὸ δένδρον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opening mentions three saved from tax collectors: Matthew and two others, one of whom is the praying tax collector (Luke 18) and the other Zacchaeus. The brief omits the praying tax collector (the one who strikes his breast) entirely, who is distinct from Zacchaeus and explicitly contrasted with him.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The barren, deadly spring of Jericho is described and interpreted as the pre-Christian church
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἡ πηγὴ αὕτη ἡ ἀφθόνως ῥέουσα, ἄχρηστον δὲ καὶ ἄγονον προχέουσα ῥεῖθρον τὸ παλαιὸν τὸν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἀποσῴζει λόγον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The spring is interpreted as 'preserving the type/word of the church' (τὸν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἀποσῴζει λόγον), not as 'the pre-Christian church' itself. It is a type/figure (λόγον) of the church, with the barrenness representing pre-Christian humanity's spiritual condition, not the church per se.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Matthew, 'The tax collector called by Jesus; Zacchaeus wishes to imitate him, though Matthew was called and obeyed while Zacchaeus takes initiative.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Μιμήσασθαι Ματθαῖον θέλω· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος τελώνης ἦν ὡς καὶ ἐγώ, ἀλλὰ Ματθαῖος μὲν οὐκ αὐθαιρέτως προσέδραμεν, ἀλλὰ κληθεὶς ὑπήκουσεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Zacchaeus wishes to imitate Matthew, but the contrast is that Matthew 'did not run of his own accord' (οὐκ αὐθαιρέτως προσέδραμεν) but 'being called, obeyed' (κληθεὶς ὑπήκουσεν). The brief's 'Zacchaeus takes initiative' overstates; Zacchaeus is still seeking to see Jesus hidden, and Christ calls him down—he does not take initiative in the same way. The key point is Zacchaeus's hidden, testing faith versus Matthew's explicit call.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Zacchaeus (interior monologue, imagined by the preacher), 'Introduced by λογισάμενος παρ' ἑαυτῷ and presented as direct speech; this is the preacher's reconstruction of Zacchaeus's thoughts, not a biblical quotation'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπεθύμησεν ἰδεῖν... λογισάμενος παρ' ἑαυτῷ· «Τίς ποτε ἆρά ἐστιν οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The interior monologue begins with ἐπεθύμησεν ἰδεῖν (he desired to see) and λογισάμενος παρ' ἑαυτῷ (reasoning to himself), but the direct speech extends far beyond what is marked, including detailed reasoning about testing whether Jesus knows hidden thoughts, and a decision to imitate Matthew. The marking is correct but incomplete—the monologue is much longer and more elaborate than indicated.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jesus, 'Introduced by λέγει αὐτῷ and direct address', sections: ['u01-rem-mid', 'u01-rem-close']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀναβλέψας λέγει αὐτῷ· Ζακχαῖε, σπεύσας κατάβηθι... Σπεύσας οὖν κατάβηθι· σήμερον γὰρ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σου δεῖ με μεῖναι
_unresolved_facts.fix: In u01-rem-mid, Jesus's speech is introduced by ἀναβλέψας λέγει αὐτῷ (looking up, he says to him). In u01-rem-close, the same words are repeated but without explicit introduction—it's a continuation/echo, not a new introduction by λέγει αὐτῷ. The brief should note the repetition and echo structure.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jesus son of Nave: Joshua son of Nun
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Greek form is Ἰησοῦς ὁ τοῦ Ναυή (Iēsous ho tou Nauē), which is 'Jesus son of Nun' or 'Joshua son of Nun'—but 'Nave' is a Latinization. The brief uses 'Nave' which is not the Greek form; the Greek has Ναυή (Nauē). The mapping should note this is the standard LXX form.
